name: Chatakpur
tagline: A forest-department eco-village at 2,400 m inside Senchal
meta_description: Chatakpur on a budget: Senchal forest eco-village at 2,400 m, the 7 km track from Sonada, homestay prices, Kanchenjunga dawns, birding and best months.
summary: Chatakpur is a forest village of about 19 houses at roughly 2,400 m inside Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, reached by a rough 7 km forest track from Sonada. Almost every family runs a homestay, at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals. Come for Kanchenjunga at dawn, birds, terraced farms and silence.

local_story.title: Nineteen houses in a 1915 sanctuary
paras: Chatakpur sits on a shelf of the Senchal ridge, the long forested spine that runs from Tiger Hill towards Sonada. Senchal was declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1915, which makes it one of the oldest in India, and its lakes still supply much of Darjeeling's drinking water. A village inside a sanctuary is unusual. Like many forest villages in these hills, Chatakpur is generally described as a settlement of families who lived and worked in the forest under the forest department, growing food on small terraces cut into the slope.

For most of the last century the village stayed poor and almost unknown. Around 2012 the forest department and the villagers' forest committee set out to turn it into an eco-village: homestays in family houses, an entry fee for visitors that goes to the forest department, organic farming on the terraces, and rules on waste and noise. Today about 19 households and roughly 90 people live here, and almost every family runs a homestay. Bookings are confirmed in advance; there is no walking in to look for a room.

What you get is a working hamlet rather than a resort. Mornings start with the Kanchenjunga massif across the northern skyline, if the cloud allows. Days are for the forest, the terraces of potatoes, maize and greens, and the medicinal herbs some families grow. By 8 pm the village is quiet, and on most nights the only sound is the wind in the trees. Come for the quiet, and leave the music speaker at home.

did_you_know: Chatakpur has only about 19 houses and roughly 90 residents, and almost every household takes guests as part of the forest department's eco-village scheme begun around 2012.
Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, which surrounds Chatakpur, was declared in 1915 and covers roughly 38–39 km²; it is among the oldest wildlife sanctuaries in India.
At about 2,400 m (7,887 ft), Chatakpur sits some 350 m higher than Darjeeling town's Chowrasta, which is why its nights are noticeably colder.
intro: Chatakpur is for people who want the Darjeeling hills without the town. It is only about 25–30 km from Darjeeling, but the last 7 km from Sonada is a rough forest track that keeps the crowds out and makes the drive part of the trip. The village is a scatter of wooden and concrete houses along a ridge, with prayer flags, vegetable terraces and the forest pressing in on all sides. On a clear morning the whole Kanchenjunga range lines up to the north.

There is not much to do here, and that is the point. Walk the forest tracks, look for birds, help in the kitchen, read, sleep early. We suggest two nights: the first evening is usually spent arriving and warming up, and two dawns double your chance of a clear view. Food is home-cooked and mostly from the village terraces. Carry warm clothes in every season, cash for everything, and a torch for the paths after dark.
facts: Patchy; signal varies by spot, plan to be offline
costs: Reserved 4x4 or Bolero, Sonada to Chatakpur
Shared jeep seat, Siliguri to Sonada
Small fee per person, collected by your homestay
Local guide for the Tiger Hill forest trail

highlights.title: Kanchenjunga from the village ridge
highlights.text: On clear mornings from October to December and in March and April, the Kanchenjunga massif fills the northern horizon from the village itself. You do not need a 4 am jeep or a crowded tower: step outside your homestay with a cup of tea at first light.

highlights.title: The forest track from Sonada
highlights.text: The 7 km track climbs from Sonada on Hill Cart Road through oak, rhododendron and tall cryptomeria. It is rough, stony and slow, about 45 minutes to an hour by 4x4, and many visitors say it is the best part of the arrival.

highlights.title: Birding in Senchal forest
highlights.text: The sanctuary's mixed broadleaf and conifer forest holds a long list of Himalayan birds. Early morning walks on the tracks around the village bring laughingthrushes, tits, warblers and, with luck, pheasants. Barking deer are heard more often than seen.

highlights.title: Terraced organic farms
highlights.text: Families grow potatoes, maize, cabbage, squash and greens on narrow terraces without chemical fertiliser, and some keep beds of medicinal herbs. Ask your host to show you round; much of what you eat at dinner was picked that afternoon.

highlights.title: The forest walk towards Tiger Hill
highlights.text: A known forest route links Chatakpur with Tiger Hill along the Senchal ridge. It is a full day on foot through the sanctuary, best done with a local guide arranged through your homestay, and only in dry weather.

highlights.title: Real quiet
highlights.text: No traffic, no shops, almost no signal. Evenings are dinner by the stove, an early night and a sky full of stars when the cloud clears. For many visitors from the plains, that is reason enough to make the trip.

how_to_reach.text: Take a Darjeeling-bound shared jeep from Siliguri or NJP and get off at Sonada on Hill Cart Road, about 16–17 km before Darjeeling; drivers usually charge the full Darjeeling fare of ₹250–350. Your homestay can arrange a 4x4 or Bolero from Sonada for the 7 km forest track, about ₹1,200–2,000 a vehicle.

From Darjeeling a reserved car costs about ₹2,500–3,500 one way, but ordinary hatchbacks and sedans should not attempt the forest track. Make sure the vehicle is a high-clearance 4x4 or Bolero. From NJP or Bagdogra budget ₹4,000–5,500 for a suitable vehicle.

Sonada is a station on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, so in theory you can ride the toy train to Sonada and be picked up there. Services and timings change with the season and track repairs: book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: All accommodation in Chatakpur is in the village's own family homestays, run under the forest department's eco-village scheme. Rooms are simple: wooden or concrete cottages, thick quilts, shared or attached bathrooms with hot water by bucket or geyser depending on the house, and meals together with the family. Expect about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. There are no hotels, shops or restaurants, so you eat where you sleep. Book ahead through the village homestay contacts or a Darjeeling agent; the forest entry fee is collected by your host.
tips: Confirm your homestay booking before you leave Sonada; visitors without one are not expected to turn up.
Use only a high-clearance 4x4 or Bolero on the forest track, and avoid it after heavy rain.
Carry enough cash for the whole stay; there is no ATM and card payments are rare.
Pack a down jacket, a warm hat and a torch even in April and October, as nights at 2,400 m are cold.
Keep noise low and carry your plastic back out; the village's place inside the sanctuary depends on it.

experiences.title: Dawn over Kanchenjunga from the ridge
experiences.summary: Watch first light turn the Kanchenjunga massif pink and then white from the edge of the village, with no crowd, no ticket and no 4 am jeep. Two mornings give you a far better chance than one.
body: Kanchenjunga, at 8,586 m the third-highest mountain on Earth, rises to the north across the deep valleys of the Rangeet and its tributaries. From Chatakpur's ridge the whole massif lines up on clear mornings, with the lesser peaks of Sikkim spread on either side. The village sits at about 2,400 m, high enough to look over much of the intervening forest, and you watch it from a homestay courtyard or a short walk up the slope.

Get up about 30 minutes before sunrise, dress warmly and take a hot drink outside; most hosts will have tea ready if you ask the night before. The first light catches the summit before anything else, turning it a pale pink, then gold; within 15–20 minutes the colour drains to white as the sun climbs and the valleys below begin to fill with light. Your host will point you to the best open spot near the house, often a terrace edge or a small rise above the village. Keep your phone or camera warm in a pocket, because batteries drain fast in the cold.

Views depend on weather far more than on the calendar. October to early December and March to April give the most clear dawns, and January and February can be very clear but bitterly cold. In the monsoon, from June to September, you are likely to see only cloud, and the forest track is at its worst. If the first morning fails, the second often works, which is one reason we suggest two nights. Even on a cloudy dawn, the mist moving through the forest below the village is worth getting up for.

faqs.q: Can you see Kanchenjunga from Chatakpur?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days the whole Kanchenjunga massif is visible from the village ridge to the north. Clear dawns are most common from October to early December and in March and April. In the monsoon from June to September cloud usually hides it. Staying two nights gives you two chances at the view.

faqs.q: Is Chatakpur better than Tiger Hill for sunrise?
faqs.a: It is quieter rather than higher. Tiger Hill, at about 2,567 m, is a little higher and on very clear days shows Everest far to the west, but it can be crowded in season. Chatakpur gives a similar Kanchenjunga view from a village courtyard with no jeeps, tickets or queues.

faqs.q: What time is sunrise at Chatakpur?
faqs.a: Roughly 4.45–5.15 am in April and May and around 6–6.20 am in December and January. Be outside about 30 minutes earlier to catch the first pink light on the summit. Ask your host the evening before; they know the timing and the best open spot near the house.

experiences.title: Forest trail along Senchal to Tiger Hill
experiences.duration: Full day, about 4–6 hours one way
experiences.best_time: Start by 7 am, Oct–Dec and Mar–Apr
experiences.cost: Guide ₹1,000–1,500 a day (indicative) · forest fees extra
experiences.summary: Walk out of Chatakpur through the oak, rhododendron and cryptomeria forest of Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary towards Tiger Hill. A full, quiet day on forest paths with a local guide, ending near Darjeeling's highest viewpoint. A car waits at the far end.
body: Chatakpur and Tiger Hill both sit on the Senchal ridge, and a forest route links them through the sanctuary. It is one of the few long walks near Darjeeling that stays almost entirely under trees. The path climbs and drops over the ridge through oak, magnolia and rhododendron, with patches of tall cryptomeria planted in the British era. In March and April the rhododendrons flower red along the way. Birds and the occasional barking deer are more common company than other walkers.

We strongly suggest going with a local guide arranged by your homestay. Paths branch without signposts, old tracks lead off in confusing directions, and mist can close in by late morning, turning a familiar ridge into a maze of grey trunks. Timings vary with route and pace, so plan a full day, carry lunch, water and a rain layer, and arrange a car to meet you at the Tiger Hill end for the drive back to Darjeeling or Ghoom. Tell your homestay your expected finish time, and keep a charged phone, even though signal comes and goes.

Rules for walking inside the sanctuary can change, and the forest department may require permission, fees or a guide for routes beyond the village. Ask your homestay when you book and check current status before you travel. Avoid the monsoon months, when leeches, landslips and slippery clay make the walk unpleasant and sometimes unsafe. The best conditions come from October to December, when the ground is dry and the air clear, and in March and April, when the rhododendrons flower. Wear proper walking shoes; trainers with worn soles are a common regret on the descent.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Chatakpur to Tiger Hill?
faqs.a: Plan a full day: most walkers take roughly 4–6 hours one way depending on route, pace and stops. Distances quoted locally vary because there is more than one path along the Senchal ridge. Start by 7 am, carry lunch and water, and arrange a car to collect you at the Tiger Hill end.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Chatakpur–Tiger Hill trail?
faqs.a: Yes, we would not do it without one. Paths fork through the sanctuary without signs, mist can drop quickly, and forest rules may require an accompanying local. Your homestay can arrange a villager who knows the route, usually for about ₹1,000–1,500 a day. Confirm the current rules when you book.

faqs.q: Is the Tiger Hill forest walk safe?
faqs.a: With a local guide in dry weather it is a reasonable walk for fit people. The risks are getting lost, slipping on wet clay and being caught in mist or rain. Black bears live in Senchal but are rarely seen. Avoid June to September, walk in daylight and tell your homestay your plan.

experiences.title: Early birding walk in Senchal forest
experiences.summary: Walk the forest tracks around Chatakpur at first light with binoculars and a villager who knows the trees. Mixed flocks, laughingthrushes and pheasants are the prize, and barking deer call from the wooded slopes below the village.
body: Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, declared in 1915, protects a band of temperate forest on the ridge above Darjeeling: oak, maple, magnolia and rhododendron, with stands of cryptomeria and bamboo. At about 2,400 m, Chatakpur sits right in the middle of this habitat, so the birding starts at your door. Mornings are best, before the mist rises from the valleys and the birds go quiet. Spring, from March to May, is the most active season, with birds singing and nesting.

Expect mixed feeding flocks moving through the canopy: tits, warblers, yuhinas and minivets, sometimes many birds of several species travelling together, with laughingthrushes scratching in the undergrowth below. Pheasants sometimes cross the forest track early in the day, and woodpeckers work the older trees. Mammals are shy; barking deer are often heard giving their sharp alarm call, and Himalayan black bears live in the sanctuary but are rarely seen. Stand still at a clearing for ten minutes and the forest tends to come to you.

Bring binoculars, a field guide or an app, and soft-coloured clothes; bright jackets and loud voices clear a forest quickly. Walk slowly and quietly on the main tracks rather than pushing into the undergrowth, which disturbs nesting birds and is where leeches wait in damp months. Some villagers know the birds well by their local names; ask your host if someone can walk with you, and agree a fee beforehand. Keep a simple list of what you see: it helps the next visitor and shows the village that birders value the forest standing.

faqs.q: What birds can I see at Chatakpur?
faqs.a: The Senchal forest around Chatakpur holds typical temperate Himalayan birds: tits, warblers, yuhinas, minivets, laughingthrushes and, with luck, pheasants on the forest tracks. Lists change with season and altitude. Spring, from March to May, is the most active time, and early mornings between 6 and 9 am are by far the best.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for birding in Senchal?
faqs.a: Visitors to Chatakpur pay a forest entry fee, collected by the homestays, which covers staying in the village. Walking on the main forest tracks near the village is normal for guests. Longer walks deeper into the sanctuary may need permission or a guide. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there wildlife danger around Chatakpur?
faqs.a: The risk is low. Barking deer are common and harmless; Himalayan black bears live in the sanctuary but keep away from people and are rarely seen. Do not walk alone at dusk or after dark, stay on known tracks, and keep food waste inside the homestay rather than leaving it outdoors.

experiences.title: Terrace farm and homestay kitchen
experiences.best_time: Late afternoon, any month the village is open
experiences.summary: Walk the village's organic terraces with your host, pick greens or potatoes for dinner, then cook alongside the family. Simple hill food: dal, rice, local greens, squash, a pickle or two, and tea at any hour.
body: Chatakpur's families farm small terraces cut into the slope around their houses, without chemical fertiliser, as part of the eco-village rules. What grows depends on the season: potatoes, maize, cabbage, radish and mustard greens, squash and its tender shoots, and beds of herbs, some grown for their medicinal use. Ask your host in the afternoon if you can walk the terraces with them. The work is done by hand, terrace by terrace, so watch rather than help unless you are invited.

Dinner in a homestay here is usually rice, dal, a vegetable or two, a fresh green, a sharp pickle and, if you ask in advance, a chicken or egg curry. In winter, look for gundruk, fermented dried greens, in a sour soup, and in season for squash shoots or fiddlehead ferns. Breakfast might be puri or bread with potato curry and eggs, and tea comes at any hour. Portions are generous and the food is mild unless you ask for the chilli pickle, which is anything but.

Cooking happens on gas or a wood stove in the family kitchen, which is also the warmest room in the house. Offer to help; most hosts are happy to show you how they make a pickle or roast maize. Tell them early about any dietary needs, because supplies have to come up the forest track from Sonada. Ask about the herbs too; some families can tell you how their elders used them, though treat that as lore rather than medicine.

faqs.q: What food is served in Chatakpur homestays?
faqs.a: Simple home-cooked hill food: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables and greens from the village terraces, pickles, and eggs or chicken if you ask in advance. Breakfast is usually puri or bread with potato curry and tea. There are no restaurants or shops in the village, so all meals come from your homestay kitchen.

faqs.q: Is Chatakpur food organic?
faqs.a: The village farms its terraces without chemical fertiliser as part of the eco-village scheme, and much of the vegetables on your plate are grown there. Rice, flour, dal, cooking gas and some other supplies come up from Sonada. So meals are largely, not entirely, from local organic produce.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians stay comfortably in Chatakpur?
faqs.a: Yes. Most everyday homestay meals are vegetarian anyway: rice, dal, vegetables, greens and pickles. Tell your host when you book if you do not eat eggs, onion or garlic, because supplies have to come up the forest track from Sonada and the kitchen needs to plan ahead.

faqs.q: Where is Chatakpur and how high is it?
faqs.a: Chatakpur is a forest village inside Senchal Wildlife Sanctuary, on the ridge between Sonada and Tiger Hill, about 25–30 km by road from Darjeeling. It sits at roughly 2,400 m (7,887 ft), a little higher than Darjeeling town, so nights are cold for most of the year.

faqs.q: How do I reach Chatakpur from NJP or Siliguri?
faqs.a: Take a Darjeeling-bound shared jeep to Sonada on Hill Cart Road, about 3 hours and ₹250–350 a seat, then a 4x4 or Bolero arranged by your homestay for the last 7 km forest track. A reserved high-clearance vehicle from NJP or Bagdogra costs roughly ₹4,000–5,500 all the way.

faqs.q: Can a normal car reach Chatakpur?
faqs.a: Not safely. The 7 km track from Sonada is rough, stony and steep, and low hatchbacks or sedans risk damage or getting stuck. Use a high-clearance 4x4 or Bolero, which homestays arrange from Sonada for about ₹1,200–2,000. After heavy rain even these can struggle, so check conditions before you go.

faqs.q: How much does a Chatakpur homestay cost?
faqs.a: Expect about ₹1,500–2,500 per person per night with dinner and breakfast, depending on the house and the season. A small forest entry fee is collected by the homestay for the forest department. Add the 4x4 from Sonada, and your total for two nights is roughly ₹5,000–7,000 per person from Sonada.

faqs.q: Do I need to book Chatakpur in advance?
faqs.a: Yes. Chatakpur runs as a forest-department eco-village with a small number of homestays, and visitors are expected to come with a confirmed booking. Arrange your stay and the 4x4 pickup from Sonada together before you leave Siliguri or Darjeeling, especially for October, November and long weekends.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Chatakpur?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest Kanchenjunga dawns and dry tracks; March and April bring rhododendron flowers and active birds. January and February are very cold, with occasional frost. Avoid June to September, when the forest track turns to mud and cloud hides the mountains most days.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and electricity in Chatakpur?
faqs.a: Power cuts are common in storms across these hills, so carry a power bank and a torch whatever your homestay says about supply. Mobile signal is patchy and varies from house to house and by network. Plan to be largely offline, and let family know before you go up the track from Sonada.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend in Chatakpur?
faqs.a: Two nights is right for most people. That gives you two chances at a clear Kanchenjunga dawn, a morning for birding, an afternoon on the terraces and a quiet evening. Add a third night if you want to walk the forest trail to Tiger Hill with a guide.

faqs.q: Is Chatakpur suitable for children and older people?
faqs.a: Yes, if they can manage cold nights and simple rooms. The bumpy 45–60 minute forest track is the hardest part. Walks around the village are gentle, but bathrooms may be shared and hot water limited. Pack thermals and ask your homestay about heaters and attached bathrooms before you book.
